summaries.summary: Biomedical annotation is costly for experts, while crowdsourcing platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk) may yield noisy lay annotations, especially for specialized technical content.
Experiments on the EBM-NLP corpus operationalize annotation difficulty, use it during training, and obtain expert annotations for difficult and randomly selected abstracts.

Item difficulty, defined as disagreement between a lay annotator or automated model and labeling, is predictable, distinct from inter-annotator agreement, and useful for improving information extraction models.
Lay annotations show lower agreement, high precision and low recall versus experts, while combining expert and lay annotations is better than lay data alone.
A system trained on combined data performs better when experts annotate difficult examples rather than instances selected at i.i.d. random.

Contributions include defining task difficulty prediction, introducing a model combining a pre-trained `universal' sentence encoder and a task-specific encoder, and improving task routing and model performance.
Crowdsourcing annotation is well studied, and considerable efforts have developed aggregation models that minimize noise inherent in such annotations.
Prior biomedical crowdsourcing work found similar expert and crowd supervision performance, unlike this work, possibly due to expert qualifications and greater task difficulty.
Prior task routing work in active learning used heterogeneous labelers, while this work operationally defines instance difficulty, predicts it, and uses it for task routing.
The application annotates randomized controlled trials (RCTs) abstracts using EBM-NLP, with 4,741 crowdsourced training abstracts and 191 expert-labeled test abstracts for p, i, o sequences.
Table 1 shows difficult examples have crowd labels distinct from expert reference annotations, while easy cases reproduce them, and difficult sentences often have complicated structure and jargon.
Sentence-level analysis uses spaCy splitting, excludes sentences with fewer than two tokens, and yields 57,505 train and 2,428 test sentences.
The test set includes crowd and domain expert annotations, with experts treated as ground truth and sentence difficulty defined by observed agreement.
Eq. 3 defines Difficulty_ti as the average over n workers of f(label_ij, y_i).
Difficulty scores average Spearmans' correlation coefficient between crowd and expert token-count vectors, with no labels maximally easy and one-sided labels maximally difficult.
Training difficulty uses 10-fold LSTM-CRF-Pattern predictions as proxy ground truth, normalized to [0, 1], with test-set Pearson's correlations of 0.57, 0.71 and 0.68.
Sentences with neither manual nor predicted annotations are maximally easy and comprise 51%, 42% and 36% for Population, Interventions and Outcomes data.
Figure 1 shows Population (p) sentence scores have a significantly lower mean than Intervention (i) and Outcome (o) scores, indicating easier annotation.
Sentences tagged by LSTM-CRF-Pattern but missed by all crowd workers receive maximally difficult score 1 and are retained as `difficult' sentences.
Because p, i and o content differs and sentences usually contain at most one type, difficulty prediction for each label type is treated separately.
The paper verifies that its difficulty definition, based on expert-crowd or model-crowd agreement, only weakly correlates with inter-annotator agreement.
Table 2 shows average agreement between domain experts is considerably higher than between crowd workers for all three label types, indicating noisier crowd annotations.
For sentences containing a reference label, Pearson's r between inter-annotator agreement and difficulty scores are 0.34, 0.30 and 0.31 for p, i and o.
Difficulty prediction is treated as a regression problem, with proposed neural model variants beginning with RNN BIBREF19 and CNN BIBREF20 models.
The universal sentence encoder (USE) BIBREF6 induces representations, and an ensemble concatenates universal and task-specific neural encoder representations before the regression layer.
Models were trained separately per label type with 300d GloVe vectors, Adam optimizer at learning rate 0.001 and decay 0.99, and batch sizes of 16.
The large universal sentence encoder with a transformer BIBREF23 was fixed, while all hyperparameters were tuned using Vizier BIBREF24 via 10-fold cross validation maximizing F1.
A baseline linear Support-Vector Regression BIBREF25 model was trained on n-gram features with n ranging from 1 to 3.
Table 3 reports Pearson correlation coefficients from 0.550 to 0.622, with all neural models outperforming baseline SVR and regression correlations lowest.
The RNN model performs strongest among stand-alone models, and combining RNN and USE further improves results, hypothesized to reflect complementary universal representations.
Correlations for Intervention and Outcomes exceed Population for all models, reflecting more uniform difficulty distributions and fewer difficult Population sentences.
Predicted difficulty is used during training to improve Population, Interventions and Outcomes information extraction by removing or re-weighting the most difficult sentences.
LSTM-CRF-Pattern on EBM-NLP BIBREF5 uses Adam with learning rate 0.001, decay 0.9, batch size 20, dropout 0.5, 200d GloVe vectors, 100d hidden char representations, and 15 epochs.
Difficult sentences are predicted via cross-fold scoring, sorted by predicted difficulty, and removed in increasing numbers before training LSTM-CRF-Pattern.
Figure 3 shows F1 marginally improves when removing difficult sentences up to 4% for Population and Interventions and 6% for Outcomes, while random removal degrades performance.
Removing a small number of the most difficult sentences modestly improves medical IE performance, but available data cannot determine how many difficult sentences should be dropped.
Sentences are re-weighted inversely to predicted difficulty using 1-a·(d_i-τ)/(1-τ), with τ set to 0.8, a set to 0.5, and LSTM-CRF-Pattern as base model.
Table 4 shows re-weighting modestly improves precision, recall and F1, with all F1 differences significant under a sign test (p<0.01) and recall improving by 10 percentage points for i and o.
Re-weighting difficult crowd-annotated sentences generally improves extraction models, presumably because performance is influenced by annotation quality.
The paper examines routing difficult instances to domain experts and easier ones to crowd annotators, contrasting difficult data with an i.i.d. random sample of the same size.

Experts re-annotate 2000 abstracts, including 1000 top-ranked difficult and 1000 randomly sampled, for interventions extraction at a cost of $3,000, with data released at https://github.com/bepnye/EBM-NLP.
Five medical experts recruited via Up-work used the BRAT toolkit BIBREF26 to highlight medical Interventions spans, with each abstract annotated by one expert and 30 abstracts examined.
Table 5 shows the expert model trained on random data has slightly better F1, higher precision and lower recall than the model trained on difficult data.
Expert-annotated data yields clearly superior F1 to crowd labels, with random crowd data 2% higher F1 than difficult crowd data and less than 1% difference for expert annotations.
The model trained on all 5k crowd-annotated abstracts has lower F1 than either expert model trained on only 20% of data, with higher precision but much lower recall.
The system now uses expert annotations for an abstract when available and otherwise crowd annotations, with results in Table 6.
Rows 1–3 describe expert-only models, including D+R using 1.75k abstracts, while Rows 4–6 describe mixed-annotation models on all 5k abstracts.
Mixing expert and crowd annotations improves F1 by at least 1 point, with difficulty-based routing giving larger gains than random expert selection.
Crowd annotations supplement expert annotations for medical IE, but the choice of one thousand difficult instances for expert annotation was uninformed.
Sending consecutive batches of most difficult examples to experts consistently increases F1 scores, mainly through increased recall rather than precision.
Re-annotating the 600 most-difficult articles reaches 68.1% F1, close to re-annotating 1000 random articles, with the trend still upward.
Neural models predicted annotation difficulty for biomedical IE with Pearson’s correlation coefficients higher than 0.45 in almost all evaluations, and an ensemble performed best.
Removing up to $\sim $ 10% of most difficult sentences did not decrease performance, while difficulty-based routing to experts and crowd annotators yielded the best results.
This work was partially supported by NSF1748771 grant, and Wallace was supported in part by NIH/NLM R01LM012086.
